newsitem.title: USA: NATO chief says alliance needs U.S. cooperation.
newsitem.headline: NATO chief says alliance needs U.S. cooperation.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana stressed the importance of the United States' role in the military alliance on Thursday and said Europe could not bear the burden of expanding NATO by itself.

"There are some Americans who argue that Europeans should pick up all of the European burden. They suggest that the burden of European security is now manageable by the Europeans alone," Solana said in a speech at the American University in Washington.
"Yet such a division of labour would run against all our shared strategic interests," he added.
Solana's comments coincide with some U.S. opposition to NATO's enlargement, which was agreed on July 8 at an alliance summit in Madrid.

The summit invited Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary to join the alliance. The entry of new members has to be approved by all of NATO's current 16 members. The Senate is expected to take up the issue next spring.
While many U.S. lawmakers support NATO's expansion plans, others argue it will be a costly process and they fear that U.S. troops might one day have to fight in Eastern Europe.

Solana said if the United States did not take part in NATO's expansion plans this would overtax the Europeans' capabilities and deprive Washington of a major source of influence in shaping the new Europe.
"And it would mean that the U.S. could not look to its traditional allies for support in global contingencies," the NATO chief said.
"So it is and remains true -- Europe needs us just as the U.S. needs Europe. As long as the United States wants to remain a global power, it will have to remain a 'European power' as well," he added.

Discussing the cost of bringing new members into NATO, Solana said he believed it would be affordable. "There is no need for these countries to arm themselves to the teeth with high-tech weaponry. After all there is no threat," he said.

Russia is strongly opposed to NATO enlargement, especially in the Baltic states. Solana said he did not think expanding NATO would isolate Russia, pointing to a special charter signed with Moscow in May that gives Russia a voice in the alliance but not a veto.
"Our desire to build a security architecture with Russia is a genuine one. And I believe we have conveyed this point to Russia convincingly," he said.
He reiterated the importance of bringing the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland into the fold. "To keep NATO closed would have perpetuated the old division of Europe."
